title: Can I claim R&D credits if I outsource my development to contractors?
description: Companies outsourcing development to contractors can often count 65% of payments for U.S. qualified research under IRC § 41.
summary: U.S. companies outsourcing development to non-employee contractors can often claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41, counting 65% of payments for qualified research performed in the United States as contract research expenses. Eligibility depends on the contract: the hiring company must sign before work begins, hold rights to the results, and pay even if the research fails.

body.text: U.S. companies outsourcing development to non-employee contractors can often claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC §41, counting 65% of payments for qualified research performed in the United States as contract research expenses. Eligibility depends on the contract: the hiring company must sign before work begins, hold rights to the results, and pay even if the research fails.
It is general information, not tax or legal advice, and readers should confirm how these rules apply to their own facts with a qualified tax professional.
1. Short answer

Yes, often. A U.S. company that pays an outside contractor (someone who is not its employee) to perform qualified research on its behalf can generally include 65% of those payments as "contract research expenses" in its qualified research expenses (QREs) under IRC §41(b)(3)(A). Whether the hiring company or the contractor gets the credit for a given piece of work depends on the contract: specifically, who bears the cost if the research fails, and who holds rights to the results. The research must also be performed in the United States, Puerto Rico or a U.S. possession.
For the company that outsources the work, the rules under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e) often point the other way:

items: Hourly (time-and-materials) or cost-reimbursement payments usually support the hiring company's claim. They do not undermine it, because the company pays whether or not the research succeeds. Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) requires that the agreement "requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful."

Payments that depend on the research succeeding are not contract research expenses for the hiring company. The regulation treats a success-contingent payment as a payment for a product or result rather than for the performance of research. Success-contingent pricing is what helps the contractor's claim instead, under the funded research rules of Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d).

body.text: Put simply, the same contract term usually cannot help both parties at once on the risk question. The party that bears the financial risk of failure for a given dollar of research is generally the party that can count that dollar.
2. The baseline requirements
2.1 The research must be qualified research

Outsourcing does not change what counts as qualified research. Under §41(d)(1), the research must meet several tests, including that it is technological in nature, that it is undertaken to develop a new or improved business component, and that substantially all of the activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation. One test changed recently. Pub. L. 119-21, title VII, §70302(b)(2)(A) (enacted July 4, 2025) amended §41(d)(1)(A). The current text requires research "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A." The prior text referred to research "with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174." Practitioner analyses (Grant Thornton, Morgan Lewis) report that new §174A and the conforming changes generally apply to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.

That is accurate only for taxable years governed by the amended statute. For earlier taxable years, including those still open for amended refund claims, the test refers to §174 "specified research or experimental expenditures." Because many outsourcing companies file refund claims for prior open years, the year-by-year distinction matters in practice.

For the hiring company, the qualified research test is applied to the research the contractor actually performs on its behalf. The company cannot satisfy the test merely by paying for development; the contractor's work must itself be technological, aimed at a new or improved business component, and conducted through a process of experimentation. That is why the hiring company needs enough visibility into the contractor's technical work to substantiate it (see section 6).
2.2 Only U.S. research counts

Research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico or any possession of the United States is excluded from qualified research (§41(d)(4)(F)). If a contract covers both domestic and offshore work, only the part attributable to qualified research performed in the United States can be counted. This applies equally when a domestic contractor subcontracts part of the work to an offshore team.
2.3 The 65% inclusion rate, and its exceptions

The general rule includes 65% of "any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research" (§41(b)(3)(A); Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(1)). The 65% haircut reflects Congress's assumption that part of every contract price covers the contractor's overhead and profit rather than research. The statute substitutes higher percentages in two narrow cases. Amounts paid to a qualified research consortium count at 75% (§41(b)(3)(C)). Amounts paid for qualified energy research to an eligible small business, an institution of higher education or a Federal laboratory count at 100% (§41(b)(3)(D)). For a typical company outsourcing software or product development to a commercial vendor, however, the 65% rate is the one that applies.

Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(1) also confirms that contract research expenses include amounts paid for services that, if performed by the taxpayer's own employees, would constitute qualified services within the meaning of §41(b)(2)(B), that is, engaging in, directly supervising or directly supporting qualified research.
3. The hiring company's tests (Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e))

The IRS Audit Techniques Guide on qualified research expenses summarizes the regulation as a three-part test. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(2), an expense is paid or incurred for the performance of qualified research only to the extent it is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement that:

headers: What it means for an outsourcing company

cells: Entered into before the research is performed
Put the agreement in place before work starts. Payment terms set after the work is done do not satisfy the test.
Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(2)(i); IRS Audit Techniques Guide
Provides that the research be performed on the taxpayer's behalf
The company must have a right to the research results. Under §1.41-2(e)(3), research can be performed on the taxpayer's behalf even if the taxpayer does not have exclusive rights to the results.
Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) and (e)(3); IRS Audit Techniques Guide
Requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful
The company must owe payment regardless of outcome. To the extent payment depends on success, it is treated as paid for the product or result and is not a contract research expense.
Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(2)(iii); IRS Audit Techniques Guide

body.text: The IRS guide also addresses vendors paid by the hour who are engaged for unspecified research. In that case the examiner looks at the work actually performed, and only the amounts attributable to qualified research count, subject to the 65% limit. The guide notes that it is current only through its June 2005 publication date, so it should be read alongside the regulation text and later case law rather than as a complete statement of current law. The IRS web page hosting it was last reviewed on July 2, 2026.

In practice, each of the three requirements is a documentation exercise. The first is satisfied by a signed master services agreement or statement of work dated before the work begins. The second is satisfied by intellectual property and deliverables clauses giving the company the right to use the results (a license is enough; outright ownership is not required). The third is satisfied by payment terms that obligate the company to pay for the research effort whether or not the technical goal is achieved.
4. The contractor's side: the funded research exclusion

Research is not qualified research "to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)" (§41(d)(4)(H)). The statute does not define "funded." The rules for deciding when the performer's research is funded are in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d). That section is titled for taxable years beginning before January 1, 1986, but courts continue to apply its funded-research rules, and in June 2026 the Tax Court expressly upheld its continued validity after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (see Smith, below).
4.1 Two conditions, both required

items: Substantial rights. If a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in the research under the agreement, the research is treated as fully funded, and none of its costs are QREs (§1.41-4A(d)(2)). Incidental benefits, such as increased experience in a field of research, are not substantial rights. A performer that must pay for the right to use the results does not hold substantial rights (§1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)).

Risk. Even when the performer retains substantial rights, its research is treated as funded to the extent of the payments it receives, except for amounts payable under the agreement that are contingent on the success of the research and are therefore considered paid for the product or result (§1.41-4A(d)(1), (d)(3)).

body.text: Without substantial rights, the research is fully funded no matter how payment is structured. With substantial rights, non-contingent payments still count as funding. In practice, a contractor needs both. The Tax Court applied the rules this way in Smith v. Commissioner (below), where the firm could claim credits only to the extent its qualified research expenses exceeded the payments it received, and only on projects where it retained substantial rights.
4.2 Why the two sides mirror each other (analysis)

The risk tests in §1.41-2(e)(2) and §1.41-4A(d)(1) are framed in opposite directions. The hiring company must bear the expense even if the research fails; the contractor avoids funding only for amounts contingent on success. The same payment term therefore tends to favor one party and disfavor the other. Rights work differently, because the hiring company does not need exclusive rights (§1.41-2(e)(3)) and the contractor needs only a substantial, not exclusive, right to use the results. A non-exclusive license back to the contractor can therefore leave both sides holding rights. That makes the risk allocation the main factor in deciding who can claim. One consequence: if a contract puts the risk of failure on the contractor but gives it no substantial rights, neither party may be able to claim the credit for that work. The hiring company fails the risk test, and the contractor fails the substantial-rights test.

body.text: 4.3 What the courts have held

items: Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995). The Federal Circuit reversed the Claims Court and held that the research was not funded. Inspection and acceptance clauses tied to detailed contract specifications meant Fairchild bore the financial risk of failure. (Summary via The Tax Adviser, March 2023.)

Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000). The right to use research results, even without exclusive rights, is a substantial right. The Tax Court relied on Lockheed Martin again in Smith (2026). (Via The Tax Adviser and Grant Thornton.)

Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015). Fixed-price contracts with milestone inspection and acceptance terms were not funded. Capped contracts with no acceptance criteria tied to payment were funded. (Via The Tax Adviser.)

United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), No. 22-30764, decided November 13, 2023. The court affirmed the district court's denial of Cajun Industries' credit (on appeal from the Middle District of Louisiana, No. 19-00596). Three sample projects failed the substantial-rights standard because the contracts transferred work product to the client. A fourth project was treated as funded even though it was a firm fixed-price contract, because the contract compensated Cajun for its expenditures.

Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), No. 23-1523, decided May 6, 2024. The court affirmed the Tax Court's summary-judgment holding (T.C. Memo. 2023-107) that the firm's research was funded. The opinion acknowledges that fixed-price contracts are more likely to be treated as unfunded. However, none of MBJ's contracts made payment contingent on research success, and a general professional standard of care did not require success.

Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (June 16, 2026), Docket Nos. 13382-17 et al. The case involved the architecture firm Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture. Practitioner reports indicate that the IRS conceded the work satisfied the four-part qualified research test, so the dispute centered on funding. The Tax Court rejected the taxpayers' Loper Bright challenge and upheld Treas. Reg. §1.41-4A(d), relying on prior Federal Circuit and Court of Federal Claims decisions and on the regulation's longevity and clarity. None of the six sample projects had payment contingent on research success, and the court found the milestone-based progress payments more closely resembled the contracts in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson. The firm retained substantial rights in four projects, through copyrights or licenses, and could claim credits only to the extent its research expenses exceeded the payments it received. In two projects it needed the client's written consent to reuse the research and therefore retained no substantial rights. The court also addressed the reasonableness of partner compensation under §174(e). (Summaries via Miller & Chevalier, July 10, 2026; KPMG; Grant Thornton, July 28, 2026; and other practitioner commentary.)

5. Worked example (hypothetical)

Hypothetical facts. A U.S. software company signs an agreement with an unrelated U.S. development firm before work starts. The company keeps the right to all results and pays $200,000 in hourly fees during the year. It also pays a $40,000 bonus that is due only if the software passes defined acceptance tests. All work is qualified research, and the firm is not the company's employee. Assume $30,000 of the hourly fees relate to work a subcontractor performed outside the United States.

cells: 1. Total paid to contractor
2. Remove the success-contingent bonus (Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(2))
3. Remove the portion for research performed outside the U.S. (§41(d)(4)(F))
4. Apply the 65% rate (§41(b)(3)(A))
$110,500 of contract research QREs

body.text: The credit is not 65% of payments, and it is not a flat percentage of QREs. Under §41(a)(1), the regular credit is 20% of the excess of QREs over a "base amount," as IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F also describes. Alternatively, a taxpayer may elect the alternative simplified credit under §41(c)(4), which equals 14% of QREs exceeding 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (6% of current-year QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of those three years). This example therefore stops at QREs.

Note also that the $40,000 success bonus excluded at step 2 is not lost to the system: if the contractor retains substantial rights in the research, that contingent amount is the portion of the contractor's research that is not funded, and the contractor may be able to count its own underlying research costs to that extent.
6. Documentation and refund claims

General recordkeeping. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d) provides that a taxpayer claiming a credit under §41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit," with record retention governed by Treas. Reg. §1.6001-1. The regulation also allows the IRS and taxpayers to agree to guidelines for keeping specific records. For an outsourcing company, eligible-expenditure records typically include the signed agreement and statements of work, invoices that separate contingent from non-contingent amounts, evidence of where the work was performed, and technical records showing the contractor's process of experimentation.

Refund-claim specificity. The IRS announced refund-claim information requirements in IR-2021-203 (October 15, 2021), following Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F. Originally, a refund claim that includes the research credit had to provide five items for each business component: the research activities performed, the individuals who performed each activity, the information each individual sought to discover, and the total qualified wage, supply and contract research expenses for the claim year (along with identification of the business components themselves). The IRS gave a grace period until January 10, 2022.

Under the IRS's research credit refund claim FAQs (updated June 18, 2024), the IRS waived two of them for refund claims postmarked after June 18, 2024: the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each sought to discover. The IRS may still request that information during an examination. Three items remain required: identify all the business components to which the claim relates for that year, identify all research activities performed for each business component, and provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (Form 6765 may be used for this). In IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), the IRS extended the transition period, during which taxpayers have 45 days to perfect a deficient refund claim before the IRS makes a final determination, through January 10, 2027. Previously that period ran through January 10, 2026.

For a company that outsources development, the third item matters directly: contract research expenses must be reported as their own total, so the company needs its 65%-adjusted contract research figure, after removing contingent and offshore amounts, ready at the time of filing.

Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (filed December 23, 2024, Docket No. 4759-22). After trial, the Tax Court concluded that an engineering firm had not engaged in qualified research. Commentary emphasizes that the firm did not show technical uncertainty or a process of experimentation. Phoenix Design was not a funded-research case. Its relevance to outsourcing is analytical: favorable contract terms do not replace technical substantiation of the research itself, and a hiring company must be able to show that the outsourced work met the qualified research tests, not merely that it paid for it under the right terms.
7. Contractor or employee?

The 65% rule applies only to payments to a person other than an employee. The IRS determines worker status under common-law rules, weighing behavioral control, financial control and the relationship of the parties. A contract label does not decide the outcome (IRS Topic No. 762; Publication 15-A). Wages paid for qualified services are counted in full as in-house research expenses under §41(b)(2)(A), with wages defined by reference to §3401(a) (§41(b)(2)(D)), not at 65%. If anything, reclassifying a worker as an employee could increase the amount counted toward QREs. The real exposure from misclassification is employment tax liability, plus the need to re-characterize the expense correctly and substantiate it as wages for qualified services.

A related point for startups: a qualified small business (generally, gross receipts under $5 million for the taxable year and no gross receipts for any taxable year before the five-taxable-year period ending with that year) may elect under §41(h) to apply part of the credit against payroll tax. The election is capped at $250,000, increased by an additional $250,000 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022. Contract research expenses count toward the credit used for this election in the same way as other QREs.
8. Other jurisdictions
8.1 United Kingdom
For accounting periods beginning on or after April 1, 2024, the merged R&D expenditure credit and enhanced R&D intensive support replaced the old SME and RDEC schemes. Under these schemes:

items: For contracted-out R&D, only the company that decides the R&D needs to be done can claim. This is generally the customer (CTA 2009 s1133).
Payments to unconnected contractors generally count at 65%.

Payments for R&D undertaken abroad generally do not qualify. Exceptions apply where necessary conditions are absent from the UK, are present where the work is done, and it would be "wholly unreasonable" to replicate them in the UK (CTA 2009 s1138A).

body.text: HMRC's guidance says whether R&D was contracted out turns on whether R&D was "intended or contemplated," not merely on the wording of the contract.
8.2 Australia

Under s355-405 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 (the "at risk" rule), an R&D entity cannot notionally deduct expenditure if, when it incurs the expenditure, it has received or could reasonably expect to receive consideration as a result of the expenditure, regardless of the results of the R&D activities. The deduction is denied where that consideration equals or exceeds the expenditure and reduced where it is less. The ATO explains the rule in Taxation Ruling TR 2021/5.
9. Practical takeaways (analysis)

items: Sign the agreement before work begins. Make it clear that your company pays for the research portion regardless of outcome and that it has a right to the results. A non-exclusive license is enough to satisfy the "on behalf of" requirement.

Keep success bonuses and acceptance-contingent payments separate in the contract and on invoices. They are excluded from your contract research expenses, and blending them with time-based fees makes the excluded portion hard to quantify on examination.
Require contractors to identify where work is performed, including work by their subcontractors, and exclude offshore portions.

Obtain enough technical documentation from the contractor (design iterations, test results, records of alternatives evaluated) to show that the outsourced work meets the qualified research tests; favorable contract terms are not a substitute (Phoenix Design Group).
Review the whole contract stack, including master agreements, statements of work and change orders, because payment and intellectual property terms may differ between documents.

If you are the contractor, a fixed price alone is not enough. You need payment expressly tied to research success, plus documented rights to use the results without paying or obtaining consent from the client.
Track contract research expenses as a separate total, because refund claims must report total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year.
